title: Chemical tests
learningObjective: describe tests for these gases: • hydrogen • oxygen • carbon dioxide • ammonia • chlorine.; describe how to carry out a flame test; know the colours formed in flame tests for these cations: • Li + is red • Na + is yellow • K + is lilac • Ca 2+ is orange-red • Cu 2+ is blue-green.; describe tests for these cations: • NH 4 + using sodium hydroxide solution and identifying the gas evolved • Cu 2+ , Fe 2+ and Fe 3+ using sodium hydroxide solution.; describe tests for these anions: • Cl – , Br – and I – using acidified silver nitrate solution • SO 4 2– using acidified barium chloride solution • CO 3 2– using hydrochloric acid and identifying the gas evolved.; describe a test for the presence of water using anhydrous copper(II) sulfate; describe a physical test to show whether a sample of water is pure

sections.title: Chemical Tests
sections.markdown:
A colourless gas pops when you hold a flame to it. Another colourless gas turns
cloudy water milky. A clear solution turns a dull green solid a brilliant blue.
None of these substances can be identified by looking at them — but each one
answers a [[chemical-test]], a procedure whose observable result has exactly one
cause. This chapter is the analytical toolkit of International GCSE chemistry:
five gas tests, the flame test and its five colours, the sodium hydroxide tests
for metal [[cation]]s and the ammonium ion, the silver nitrate, barium chloride
and acid tests for three families of [[anion]]s, and the two tests for water —
one chemical, one physical. Every test follows the same logic: add the reagent,
watch for the positive result, and name the ion or gas it proves.

Seven objectives organise the chapter, and every one of them is examined in
both papers. The gas tests (2.44) are pure observation questions. The flame
test (2.45) and its colour table (2.46) are method-and-recall questions. The
cation tests (2.47) and anion tests (2.48) are the descriptive essay questions
of this chapter — full marks live in the sequence of additions and the colour
of each result. The two water tests (2.49 and 2.50) close the chapter by
distinguishing *presence* of water from *purity* of water, a distinction the
examiner likes to probe. Learn each test as a three-line script — reagent,
result, conclusion — and the whole chapter compresses into one page you can
reproduce under exam conditions.

:::prior-knowledge
Four earlier chapters load this one. From Chapter 12 (u2:c12) you need the
halogens and their coloured silver salts in embryo; the halide tests here are
the payoff of Group 7 chemistry. From Chapter 11 (u2:c11) you need the alkaline
metals — lithium, sodium and potassium — whose flame colours and hydroxide
solubility decide two of the tests. From Chapter 17 (u2:c17) you need the
solubility rules, because every positive result in the cation and anion tests
is an insoluble salt precipitating out of solution; the term precipitate was
defined there. From Chapter 5 (u1:c05) you need balanced equations
with state symbols — (s), (l), (g), (aq) — because writing the ionic equation
for a precipitate is a standard follow-up mark here.
:::

:::exam-hint
All seven objectives are assessed in both Paper 1C and Paper 2C — nothing in
this chapter is chemistry-only. The recurring question shapes are: name the
gas from a described observation ("a green gas that bleaches damp litmus");
describe a test in full, including the reagent, the observation and the
positive result; interpret a table of test results to identify an unknown
compound; and write the ionic equation for a precipitate. Watch the command
words: *describe* wants the procedure in order, *state* wants the single
observation, *explain* wants the chemistry behind the result — for example why
the acid must be added *before* the barium chloride in the sulfate test.
:::

:::misconception
"'Chemical tests' are separate facts to memorise, unrelated to the reactions
of earlier chapters." Every test in this chapter is a reaction you already
know, pointed at a question. The limewater test for carbon dioxide *is* the
calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide reaction; the cation tests *are* the
insoluble-hydroxide entries of the solubility rules; the halide tests *are*
precipitation reactions between silver ions and Group 7 ions. Learn the
reaction and the test is the reaction plus one observation.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.44–2.50 orientation items. Before moving on, say in
one sentence what makes a procedure a [[chemical-test]] (one reagent, one
observable, one conclusion), name the two ion classes the chapter tests for,
and state which test distinguishes *pure* water from merely *wet* matter. If
you can also list the five gases in objective 2.44 from memory, the chapter's
map is already in your head.
:::

sections.title: Tests for Hydrogen and Oxygen Gases
sections.markdown:
Two gases in this chapter announce themselves with a flame. Hydrogen is
identified with a **lighted splint** held to the mouth of the tube: the
hydrogen explodes with a **squeaky pop**. The pop is genuine combustion — the
hydrogen combines explosively with oxygen from the air to make water, and it
is the rapid expansion of the burning gas mixture that you hear:

2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)

Oxygen is identified with a **glowing splint** placed inside the tube of gas:
oxygen **relights a glowing splint**. The reasoning is the same chemistry from
the other side — combustion needs oxygen, so a gas that rekindles a flame that
had almost died is oxygen-rich. Note the pairing of the two tests: a *lighted*
splint finds the gas that burns, a *glowing* splint finds the gas that lets
other things burn. Mixing the splints up is the classic lost mark, so anchor
each test to its adverb.

Both tests are safe on test-tube quantities, but the hydrogen pop is a genuine
mini-explosion, so the tube mouth must point away from faces and the splint
must be held at the mouth, not lowered inside. If the pop is faint or absent,
the gas may have escaped or been displaced by air — collect a fresh sample
rather than concluding the gas is not hydrogen.

:::exam-hint
The examiner expects both tests word-perfect: hydrogen — lighted splint,
squeaky pop; oxygen — glowing splint, relights. A favourite extended version
gives you three colourless gases (hydrogen, oxygen and air) and asks you to
identify each with the splint tests: the pop identifies hydrogen, the relight
identifies oxygen, and the splint that simply goes out leaves air, whose 21%
oxygen is too dilute to relight the splint. If asked for the equation, the
hydrogen pop gives 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) — balanced, with state symbols.
:::

:::misconception
"A positive squeaky pop proves the tube contains *pure* hydrogen." A pop
confirms hydrogen is present, but hydrogen only explodes cleanly when mixed
with air — pure hydrogen in a tube that never met air burns quietly or not at
all. Equally, the pop test does not identify hydrogen uniquely among all
conceivable gases; it identifies hydrogen among the gases you will meet. Say
"squeaky pop with a lighted splint, so hydrogen" — the full script is what
earns the mark.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.44 gas-test items. Cover the section and reconstruct
both scripts: which splint for hydrogen and what do you hear; which splint for
oxygen and what do you see? Then write the equation for the hydrogen pop with
state symbols, and explain in one sentence why air fails the glowing-splint
test.
:::

sections.title: The Test for Carbon Dioxide Gas
sections.markdown:
Bubble the gas through **limewater**. Carbon dioxide turns limewater **milky**
— some mark schemes say chalky or cloudy; all three words describe the same
thing, a fine white solid forming and scattering the light.

[[limewater]] is calcium hydroxide solution, and the milkiness is a genuine
precipitation reaction. The carbon dioxide reacts with the calcium hydroxide
to form a white precipitate of calcium carbonate:

Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l)

This is the same carbonate chemistry you met in the salt preparations: an
alkaline solution meeting an acidic oxide, with an insoluble salt as the
product. The observation and the equation are two halves of one mark scheme
line, so learn them joined.

:::key-point
If you keep bubbling the carbon dioxide through the limewater, the white
precipitate will eventually disappear again. This is because the CO₂ reacts
with the calcium carbonate to form calcium [[hydrogencarbonate]], which is
soluble in water:

CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) → Ca(HCO₃)₂(aq)

So a positive test has a shelf life: stop bubbling once the milkiness appears,
or over-running the test dissolves your own evidence.
:::

:::exam-hint
The full script is: bubble the gas through limewater; the limewater turns milky
or cloudy; therefore carbon dioxide. The follow-up asks are predictable and
worth preparing: give the equation for the precipitate (Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃
+ H₂O, with state symbols); name the white precipitate (calcium carbonate); and
explain why the milkiness vanishes if bubbling continues (soluble calcium
hydrogencarbonate forms). That last explanation is the distinguisher between a
competent answer and a top answer — quote the hydrogencarbonate equation if you
want the respect line.
:::

:::misconception
"Limewater is lime juice, or somehow the same as water." Limewater is calcium
hydroxide solution, Ca(OH)₂(aq) — an alkali, nothing like fruit juice. The test
works *because* the calcium hydroxide reacts with the acidic oxide CO₂ to make
the insoluble carbonate; plain water would form no precipitate and prove
nothing. Also resist saying "limewater turns carbon dioxide milky" — the gas
turns the *limewater* milky; keep the subject and object the right way round.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.44 gas-test items. Reconstruct the three-line script
(reagent, observation, conclusion) for carbon dioxide; write the precipitation
equation with state symbols; and explain in one sentence what happens if you
bubble CO₂ for too long, with the equation for the dissolving step.
:::

sections.title: The Test for Chlorine Gas
sections.markdown:
Hold a piece of **damp litmus paper** (or damp universal indicator paper) at
the mouth of the tube or inside it. Chlorine **bleaches** the damp litmus
paper — it turns the paper white. To [[bleach]] is to strip colour, and
chlorine is the only gas you will meet that does it.

The dampness matters. Chlorine dissolves in the water on the wet paper and
reacts with it; dry paper is a much weaker positive result. And the order of
colour changes tells you two things at once. If **blue** litmus or universal
indicator paper is used, it goes **red first** — the chlorine dissolves in the
water to form an acidic solution — and **then white**, as the bleaching
follows. Red-then-white on blue litmus is the complete chlorine signature:
acidic *and* bleaching in one observation.

Chlorine is a green gas, so the colour of the gas itself is a supporting clue,
but never a conclusion: name gases by their tests, not by their colour.

:::safety
Wear eye protection. Avoid inhaling or "sniffing" chlorine or ammonia,
especially if you have a breathing problem such as asthma. Both gases are
tested at the mouth of the tube, not by leaning over it.
:::

:::exam-hint
Write the script in order: damp litmus paper at the mouth of the tube; blue
litmus goes red first then white (or colourless litmus simply turns white);
therefore chlorine. The two-stage colour change is the mark-winner — answers
that only say "bleaches litmus" drop the acidity half. A classic distractor
pairs this test with the ammonia test: ammonia turns damp *red* litmus *blue*
(alkaline), chlorine turns damp *blue* litmus *red then white* (acidic then
bleached). Learn the pair together and neither can be confused with the other.
:::

:::misconception
"Chlorine turns litmus white, so it is an alkali like ammonia." The bleaching
is not an acid-base colour flip — it is a chemical destruction of the dye,
which is why the paper does not turn back. Chlorine's first effect on damp
blue litmus is actually acidic (red), from the acidic solution it forms with
the water on the paper; the whitening that follows is the bleach. Alkalis
turn litmus blue without destroying it. Two different mechanisms, two
different colours, one discipline: quote both stages.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.44 gas-test items. State the full chlorine test with
the two-stage colour change on blue litmus, then answer in one sentence each:
why must the paper be damp, and why does the paper go red before it goes white?
Finish by contrasting the ammonia test in a single paired sentence.
:::

sections.title: The Test for Ammonia Gas
sections.markdown:
Hold a piece of **damp universal indicator paper or red litmus paper** at the
mouth of the test-tube. Ammonia turns the paper **blue**. It is the only gas
you will meet at International GCSE that is alkaline, so a damp indicator
paper turning blue at the mouth of a tube is ammonia and nothing else.

The chemistry is the ammonia-as-[[alkali]] story from the acids and bases
chapter: dissolved ammonia reacts reversibly with water to generate hydroxide
ions, NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, and it is those hydroxide ions that flip the
indicator. The dampness of the paper is essential for the same reason as in
the chlorine test — the gas must dissolve in the water on the paper before it
can show its alkaline character.

Keep the two damp-paper tests locked together in your memory: ammonia turns
damp **red** litmus **blue** (alkaline); chlorine turns damp **blue** litmus
**red, then white** (acidic, then bleached). One gas goes up the pH scale,
the other crashes down it and destroys the dye on the way.

:::exam-hint
The script: hold damp red litmus paper (or universal indicator paper) at the
mouth of the tube; it turns blue; therefore ammonia. The examiner's favourite
extension connects this test to the cation tests later in the chapter — when
you warm an ammonium compound with sodium hydroxide solution, the ammonia gas
evolved is identified by exactly this test. So the damp-red-litmus script
appears twice in exam questions: once as the gas test here, once as the
confirmation step in the ammonium-ion test. Write it identically both times.
:::

:::misconception
"Ammonia solution and ammonia gas are the same thing, so the gas test needs a
solution." The gas is tested at the mouth of the tube with damp paper; the
*solution* is the laboratory reagent you met in titrations. They share the
alkaline character because the same reversible reaction with water happens in
both — on the wet paper and in the bottle — but the test for the *gas* never
involves dissolving the sample first. Also, "ammonia turns litmus blue" is
incomplete without *damp*: dry paper gives a weak or absent result.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.44 gas-test items. Give the full ammonia test
script, state why ammonia is uniquely identifiable among the course's gases by
this one observation, and explain in one sentence what the damp paper
contributes. Then pair it from memory with the chlorine result on the same
kind of paper.
:::

sections.title: Testing for Water
sections.markdown:
Water has two tests, and they answer two different questions. The first asks
*is water present?*; the second asks *is this sample pure water?* Mixing them
up is the single most-tested trap in this section.

**The chemical test for the presence of water (2.49):** add the sample to
white [[anhydrous]] copper(II) sulfate. Water turns it **blue**. Anhydrous
copper(II) sulfate lacks its [[water-of-crystallisation]] and is white;
dropping water onto it replaces the water of crystallisation and the solid
turns blue as the [[hydrated]] compound CuSO₄·5H₂O forms. The colour flip is
fast, cheap and unmistakable — white to blue means water.

The same test, however, works for anything that contains water. Sodium
chloride solution turns it blue; dilute sulfuric acid turns it blue; damp
sand turns it blue. A positive result proves the presence of water — it does
**not** show that the water is pure, because the test never looks at what
*else* is dissolved in the sample.

**The physical test for purity (2.50):** measure the **freezing (melting)
point or the boiling point**. Pure water freezes at exactly 0 °C and boils at
exactly 100 °C at 1 atmosphere pressure. If the water is impure, it will
usually freeze at a **lower** temperature and boil at a **higher** temperature
— the dissolved substances spread the phase changes away from the fixed
points. This is a physical test: nothing is identified chemically, the
temperatures themselves are the evidence.

:::safety
Avoid skin contact with the copper salts — anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is
irritant as well as an indicator of water. Wear eye protection throughout.
:::

:::exam-hint
The examiner pairs these tests precisely to punish the impure/pure confusion.
A typical question: "A liquid turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue. Does
this prove the liquid is pure water? Explain." The full-mark answer is no —
the blue flip shows water is present, and impure water would turn it blue just
as happily; purity needs the melting/boiling-point measurement. Quote both
fixed numbers (0 °C and 100 °C at 1 atmosphere) and both drift directions
(impure water freezes lower, boils higher). If you also explain *why* —
dissolved substances lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point —
you have the whole mark scheme in four sentences.
:::

:::misconception
"The copper(II) sulfate test proves water is pure because it gives such a
clear result." Clarity of result is not purity of conclusion. The white-to-blue
flip is a test for the **presence** of water molecules, full stop — it fires
identically for seawater, acid solution and rainwater. Only the physical
measurement (exact freezing or boiling point) speaks about purity. The two
objectives are numbered separately in the specification for exactly this
reason.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.49–2.50 water-test items. State the chemical test
(white solid, colour change, product) and the physical test (two fixed
temperatures, two drift directions). Then answer the trap question cold: a
liquid turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue *and* boils at 102 °C — is it
pure water, and what does each observation prove?
:::

sections.title: Testing for Ions: Flame Tests
sections.markdown:
Every salt contains at least one cation and one anion, and the two ion classes
are tested separately. The [[flame-test]] is the first of the cation tests: it
shows the presence of certain metal ions in a compound, because those ions
colour a flame in ways the naked eye can tell apart.

The method has four moves. First, a **platinum or nichrome wire** is dipped
into **concentrated hydrochloric acid**. Second, the wire is dipped into the
salt you want to test, so that some salt sticks to the end. Third, the wire
and its salt are held just within a [[non-luminous-flame]] — the
non-luminous (roaring) Bunsen burner flame. Fourth, the colour is observed and matched to the ion it proves.

The concentrated hydrochloric acid is not decoration — it cleans the wire.
A new wire, or one reused from an earlier test, is cleaned by dipping it into
the concentrated acid and then holding it in the non-luminous flame, repeated
until the wire gives no colour to the flame at all. Only a colour-clean wire
gives a result you can trust: any leftover sodium from a previous test, for
example, would paint its own yellow over the truth. The acid converts surface
contamination into volatile chlorides that the flame strips away, which is
why the cleaning dip and the test dip use the same reagent.

:::key-point
If a new piece of wire is not being used, it is usually cleaned by dipping it
into concentrated hydrochloric acid and then holding it in a non-luminous
Bunsen flame. This is repeated until the wire does not give any colour to the
flame.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection and take great care with the concentrated acid. Do not
get it on your skin, and watch out for "spitting" when heating it on the wire
— hold the wire at arm's length in the flame.
:::

:::exam-hint
Method questions on this test are scored on the *sequence*, so rehearse it as
four numbered moves: acid, salt, non-luminous flame, colour. The two details
examiners most want are the **concentrated hydrochloric acid** (name it fully
— "acid" alone is loose) and the **non-luminous** flame (the blue roaring
flame, not the yellow safety flame — the yellow flame's own colour would
drown the result). A common follow-up asks *why* the wire is cleaned first:
to remove ions from earlier tests that would give their own flame colours.
That "why" is one mark that costs one sentence.
:::

:::misconception
"You dip the wire in the acid to make the salt stick better." The acid dip
has two jobs and adhesion is the lesser one. Its primary job is cleaning:
concentrated hydrochloric acid converts contaminating ions on the wire into
volatile chlorides that burn away in the flame, leaving no colour of their
own. Without the clean, a wire that once touched sodium chloride would report
yellow for every sample afterwards — the previous test contaminating the next
one.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.45 method items. Recite the four moves in order
with the two non-negotiable details (concentrated HCl, non-luminous flame);
explain in one sentence why the wire is cleaned until it gives no colour; and
state which flame on a Bunsen burner is used and why the other one would
spoil the test.
:::

sections.title: Flame Colours of the Cations
sections.markdown:
A clean [[flame-test]] reports its cation by colour. Five cations are
examined, and the five colours are pure recall — the specification words are
the mark scheme words:

| Cation | Flame colour |
|---|---|
| Li⁺ | red |
| Na⁺ | yellow |
| K⁺ | lilac |
| Ca²⁺ | orange-red |
| Cu²⁺ | blue-green |

Two colour pairs need guarding. **Red versus orange-red**: lithium burns red,
calcium burns orange-red — the "orange" half of calcium's description is what
separates it from lithium's clean red. **Yellow versus everything yellow-ish**:
sodium's yellow is famously intrusive, and that is precisely why the wire
cleaning of the previous section matters — a contaminated wire reports sodium
for every sample it meets.

The colours come from the electrons of the metal ions: the flame's energy
promotes electrons to higher levels, and the light they emit falling back has
wavelengths — colours — fixed by the ion's identity. That is why the test
identifies the *ion*: the same element carries the same electron
arrangement whatever compound it sits in.

:::key-point
Lithium is not the only ion to give a red flame colour. Strontium gives a very
similar colour. The only way to be sure is to compare the flame colour
alongside that of a known compound of lithium or strontium.
:::

:::exam-hint
The colour for sodium is described as yellow in the specification, but you
will also see it described as orange — both are usually accepted. For every
other colour, stay with the specification's exact word: red, lilac,
orange-red, blue-green. "Purple" for potassium loses the mark that "lilac"
earns. Expect two question shapes: a table to complete (ion to colour or
colour to ion) and a describe-the-test question that wants the method *plus*
the colour word *plus* the conclusion. Drill the five pairs until the table
rebuilds itself on paper in under thirty seconds.
:::

:::misconception
"The flame colour tells you the compound, so lithium chloride and lithium
sulfate give different colours." The colour belongs to the **cation**, not the
compound: every lithium salt burns red, every copper(II) salt burns
blue-green, because the emitting electrons belong to the metal ion. That is
what makes the test a cation test. The anion is invisible to the flame —
which is exactly why the anion tests later in this chapter exist.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection for all these tests and avoid skin contact with the
reactants and products. Carry out flame tests in a well-ventilated space and
never re-heat a wire whose acid drop has not burned off.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.46 recall items. Rebuild the five-row colour table
from memory, then answer: which two cations are most easily confused and what
distinguishes their colours; which specification colour word has one accepted
synonym; and why does the colour identify the ion rather than the compound?
:::

sections.title: Testing for Cations Using Sodium Hydroxide Solution
sections.markdown:
The flame test covers five cations; sodium hydroxide solution covers the
rest. The idea rests on one solubility fact: of the common hydroxides, only
those of sodium, potassium and ammonium dissolve in water to any extent. Most
metal hydroxides are [[insoluble]]. So when you add sodium hydroxide solution
to a solution containing metal ions, the metal's hydroxide forms and drops out
of solution as a solid — a [[precipitate]] — and the **colour** of that
precipitate names the metal.

To carry out the test, dissolve the salt in distilled (pure) water and put
about 1 cm³ in a test-tube. Add about the same volume of dilute sodium
hydroxide solution. What you are looking for in most of these tests is the
formation of a precipitate; the solution goes cloudy as the solid forms.

**A blue precipitate** shows the presence of **copper(II) ions**. The
precipitate is copper(II) hydroxide. Any copper(II) salt in solution reacts
this way — with copper(II) sulfate solution, the full equation is:

CuSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq)

**An orange-brown precipitate** shows the presence of **iron(III) ions
(Fe³⁺)**. The precipitate is iron(III) hydroxide. Any iron(III) compound in
solution gives this precipitate — for example:

FeCl₃(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3NaCl(aq)

**A green precipitate** shows the presence of **iron(II) ions (Fe²⁺)**. The
precipitate is iron(II) hydroxide — say, from iron(II) sulfate solution:

FeSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq)

Notice how much more complicated the full equations are than the story they
tell — they also hide what is happening. The [[ionic-equation]] shows only the
things that actually react, and for precipitation reactions it is the better
tool:

Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)  ·  Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s)

:::key-point
The green precipitate darkens on standing and turns orange-brown around the
top of the tube. This is because the iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised to
iron(III) hydroxide by the air.
:::

:::key-point
You must carry out these three tests on a **solution** of the salt you are
testing. If you tested the solid you would not be able to see whether a
precipitate had formed, because there is already solid present.
:::

:::exam-hint
The three coloured precipitates are the heart of 2.47: blue = Cu²⁺, green =
Fe²⁺, orange-brown = Fe³⁺. Two follow-up marks recur. First, the *why-a-
solution* point: the test needs a solution because a solid sample would hide
its own precipitate — ammonium is the exception examined next section, where
the evidence is a gas, not a colour. Second, the ionic equation: for any
named metal hydroxide precipitate, write the metal ion and hydroxide ions as
aqueous and the hydroxide as solid, balanced — Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂,
Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂, Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃. Learn the three charge-to-
hydroxide ratios (1:2, 2:2, 3:3) and the balancing is automatic.
:::

:::misconception
"A green precipitate could be iron(II) or iron(III) — they sound similar." The
colours are different and the difference is the whole test: iron(II) hydroxide
is **green**; iron(III) hydroxide is **orange-brown**. There is a bridge
between them, though — the green precipitate darkens on standing and turns
orange-brown from the top of the tube downwards, because air oxidises Fe²⁺ to
Fe³⁺. If the question shows that colour change over time, it is telling you
the sample was iron(II), slowly rusting in the test-tube.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.47 cation-test items. Rebuild the colour table for
Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ with the name and formula of each precipitate; write the
ionic equations for all three; and answer the method question — why must the
test use a solution, and what would you see if iron(II) hydroxide were left
standing?
:::

sections.title: The Test for Ammonium Ions
sections.markdown:
Sodium hydroxide solution reacts with **ammonium** salts — either solid or in
solution — to produce **ammonia gas**. This is the fourth cation test of
objective 2.47, and it breaks the pattern of the other three: there is no
precipitate to look for, because ammonium hydroxide does not form a solid.
The evidence is a gas with a smell and an alkaline reaction.

In the cold, just enough ammonia is produced for the test to work by smell —
the sharp, familiar odour of the reagent bottle. If you **warm** the mixture,
ammonia comes off steadily and can be tested properly with a piece of **damp
red litmus paper or universal indicator paper**: ammonia is alkaline and turns
the paper **blue** — the gas test from earlier in this chapter, reused as the
confirmation step here.

The ionic equation is:

NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → NH₃(g) + H₂O(l)

A full equation for adding sodium hydroxide solution to solid ammonium
chloride is:

NH₄Cl(s) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + NH₃(g) + H₂O(l)

This test works on a sample of a solid or a solution, because you are not
looking for a precipitate — the solid reacts just as well as its solution.

:::key-point
Recognising gases by smelling them has to be done with great care. In this
case there is usually so little ammonia gas present in the cold that it is
safe to smell if you take the normal precautions. You should not, however,
make any attempt to smell the mixture when it is warm.
:::

:::safety
Do not attempt to smell the ammonia gas if you have a breathing problem such
as asthma. Waft gently towards the nose if a smell is required at all, and
carry out the warming step in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated space.
:::

The reactions of the four cations with sodium hydroxide solution compress
into one summary table:

| Ion | Result of adding NaOH(aq) | Name of precipitate formed | Formula of precipitate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cu²⁺ | blue precipitate | copper(II) hydroxide | Cu(OH)₂ |
| Fe²⁺ | green precipitate | iron(II) hydroxide | Fe(OH)₂ |
| Fe³⁺ | orange-brown precipitate | iron(III) hydroxide | Fe(OH)₃ |
| NH₄⁺ | ammonia gas produced (damp red litmus turns blue) | no precipitate | — |

:::exam-hint
The ammonium test is the only 2.47 test whose evidence is a gas, and the
mark scheme wants the whole chain: add sodium hydroxide and warm; ammonia gas
evolved; identified by damp red litmus turning blue. Expect the ionic equation
(NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O) as a one-mark rider — note that the ammonium ion
*is* the acid-side partner here, handing a proton to the hydroxide base. The
summary table above is the single most examinable artefact of the cation
section: cover the right-hand columns and reconstruct all four rows until you
can do it cold.
:::

:::misconception
"The ammonium test works like the copper test — add sodium hydroxide and
watch for a coloured solid." There is no coloured solid: [[ammonium-ion]]
hydroxide does not precipitate, it decomposes to ammonia and water. That is
also why this test uniquely accepts a solid sample — with the metal hydroxide
tests, a solid sample would hide its precipitate; here the ammonia gas escapes
whether the sample is solid or dissolved. Write "no precipitate; ammonia
evolved" in that order and the mark scheme finds you.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.47 cation-test items. State the ammonium test as a
three-step script (reagent + warm, gas, confirmation), write both equations,
and fill in the fourth row of the cation summary table from memory. Explain in
one sentence why this test — alone among the four — can be run on a solid.
:::

sections.title: Testing for Carbonates
sections.markdown:
The anion tests begin with the easiest: add dilute hydrochloric acid to your
sample and look for **fizzing/bubbling**. A [[carbonate]] releases carbon
dioxide gas when it meets an acid, and the identity of the gas is confirmed by
bubbling it through limewater, which turns milky — the gas test from earlier
in this chapter closing the loop on the anion side.

Most carbonates are insoluble in water, so you will usually be doing this test
on a sample of a **solid**. The soluble carbonates — sodium carbonate,
potassium carbonate and ammonium carbonate — are the exception, and the test
works equally well on solutions of these. Either way the reaction is the same:
carbonate plus acid gives salt plus water plus carbon dioxide. For example,
with zinc carbonate and dilute nitric acid:

ZnCO₃(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

The ionic equation shows any carbonate reacting with any acid:

CO₃²⁻(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

That generality is the point of the test: every carbonate, solid or dissolved,
does the same thing to an acid, so one fizz-and-confirm script covers them all.

:::exam-hint
The full script is: add dilute hydrochloric acid; fizzing/bubbling observed;
bubble the gas through limewater; limewater turns milky; therefore a carbonate
is present. Both halves matter — fizzing alone is not proof (other chemistry
can make bubbles), and the limewater confirmation is the mark that converts
"gas evolved" into "carbon dioxide identified". The ionic equation
CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O is the extension-level mark: quote it when asked how
*all* carbonates behave. And mind the state symbols — the carbonate is solid
here, the hydrogen ions aqueous.
:::

:::misconception
"Fizzing with an acid proves carbonate, full stop." Fizzing proves a *gas* is
evolved; the limewater step proves it is *carbon dioxide*. The two-step
structure is not bureaucracy — metals above hydrogen also fizz with acids
(hydrogen, which pops, not milks). If a question hands you an unknown white
powder that fizzes with acid, the carbonate conclusion is only earned when the
gas turns limewater milky. Quote both observations and the conclusion writes
itself.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection for all these tests and avoid skin contact with the
reactants and products. Point the mouth of the tube away from you when adding
acid to a solid.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.48 anion-test items. Give the two-step carbonate
script and the reason the second step exists; write the ionic equation that
covers every carbonate; and state which three carbonates are soluble enough to
be tested in solution. Then predict: what would you observe adding dilute
hydrochloric acid to calcium carbonate, and how would you confirm the gas?
:::

sections.title: Testing for Sulfates
sections.markdown:
Make a solution of your suspected [[sulfate]] in distilled (pure) water, add
some **dilute hydrochloric acid**, and then add some **barium chloride
solution**. A sulfate produces a **white precipitate** of barium sulfate:

Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

The ionic equation is one line, but the *order* of the additions is the
examined thinking. The acid goes in first to react with and remove other
anions that might also produce white precipitates with the barium chloride.
The classic interferer is the carbonate: barium carbonate is white and
insoluble, so without the acid step, carbonate ions in the sample would fake
a positive sulfate result. The acid reacts with the carbonate ions and
removes them — the fizz of carbon dioxide escaping is the interference being
destroyed — and only then does the barium chloride report on sulfate alone.
The acid must be added **before** the barium chloride solution; reversed, the
false precipitate has already formed.

One acid is forbidden in this test. You must never acidify the solution with
**sulfuric acid**, because sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions — add those and
a barium sulfate precipitate is guaranteed regardless of the sample. The test
would be reporting on the reagent, not the unknown.

:::key-point
You could also use nitric acid and barium nitrate solution in the same way.
:::

:::exam-hint
The script: dilute hydrochloric acid first, then barium chloride solution;
white precipitate; sulfate present. The two "why" follow-ups are where the
marks live: *why acid first?* — to remove carbonate (and other interfering)
ions that would give a white barium precipitate of their own; *why not
sulfuric acid?* — it would add sulfate ions and force a positive result.
Both answers are one sentence each and both have appeared in real papers.
Name the white precipitate (barium sulfate) and quote its ionic equation with
state symbols; the nitric acid + barium nitrate variant earns credit when
offered as an alternative pair.
:::

:::misconception
"The acid step is just to help the salt dissolve — any acid will do." The acid
is not a solvent aid; it is a *bodyguard* that destroys interfering anions
before the barium ion arrives. And the acid choice is not free: sulfuric acid
would introduce the very ion being tested for, guaranteeing a white
precipitate even in a sulfate-free sample. Hydrochloric acid (chloride salts
of barium stay soluble) or nitric acid (nitrate salts all soluble) are safe;
sulfuric acid never is.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.48 anion-test items. Recite the sulfate script in
order with the observation and conclusion; write the ionic equation; and give
one-sentence answers to both "why" questions — acid before barium chloride,
and never sulfuric acid. Then state the alternative reagent pair.
:::

sections.title: Testing for Halides
sections.markdown:
The halide test closes the anion family: chloride, bromide and iodide ions are
caught with silver nitrate, and the **colour of the silver halide precipitate**
says which one. The [[halide-ion]]s — the −1 ions formed by the halogens of
Group 7 — are collectively named by this test's logic: one reagent, three
colours, three conclusions.

Make a solution of your suspected chloride, bromide or iodide and add enough
dilute nitric acid to make it [[acidified]]. Then add some **silver nitrate
solution**.

A **white** precipitate (of silver chloride) shows the presence of **chloride
ions**:

Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)

A **cream** precipitate (of silver bromide) shows the presence of **bromide
ions**:

Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s)

A **yellow** precipitate (of silver iodide) shows the presence of **iodide
ions**:

Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s)

The nitric acid is doing the same bodyguard work as in the sulfate test: it
reacts with and removes other anions that would also form precipitates with
silver nitrate — carbonate and hydroxide ions are the named offenders. But the
acid choice is even tighter here. You must **not** use hydrochloric acid (nor
hydrobromic nor hydroiodic acid), because you would be adding halide ions of
your own and a precipitate is then certain — the test would report the
reagent. Nitric acid contributes only nitrate ions, whose silver salt stays
dissolved.

:::key-point
All of these silver halide precipitates tend to discolour to greys and pale
purples on exposure to light.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection for all these tests and avoid skin contact with the
reactants and products. Silver nitrate stains skin black on contact — handle
the solution, not the drops.
:::

:::exam-hint
The three colours in specification language: chloride **white**, bromide
**cream**, iodide **yellow**. "Off-white" for chloride loses to "white"; the
white-cream-yellow sequence darkens down the group, which is a memory hook
the examiner rewards when you volunteer it. The equation set is three ionic
equations differing only in the halide — learn one and you know all three.
Two follow-ups recur: *why nitric acid?* (removes carbonate/hydroxide
interference without adding halide ions) and *why not hydrochloric acid?*
(its chloride ions would precipitate silver chloride regardless of the
sample). Both are one-sentence answers worth preparing verbatim.
:::

:::misconception
"Any dilute acid will do for the acidified step — acid is acid." In the
halide test the acid's own anion joins the reaction mixture, so the wrong acid
fakes the result: hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions, hydrobromic adds
bromide, hydroiodic adds iodide — each certain to precipitate with silver
nitrate. Compare the sulfate test, where the forbidden acid was sulfuric for
the same structural reason (its anion was the target ion). The rule generalises:
never acidify with an acid whose anion is the ion you are testing for.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.48 anion-test items. Rebuild the three-row table
(halide, precipitate colour, formula, ionic equation); state why nitric acid
is used and why the hydrohalic acids are banned; and explain what you would
see if a silver nitrate solution were added to a sample that had been
acidified with hydrochloric acid by mistake.
:::

sections.title: Summary of the Anion Tests
sections.markdown:
Three [[anion]] families, three scripts, one table. Everything the carbonate,
sulfate and halide sections taught compresses into this summary, and the
compression is itself the revision: cover the right-hand columns, rebuild
each row, and the whole of objective 2.48 is one artefact.

| Ion | Test | Positive result | Product of reaction |
|---|---|---|---|
| CO₃²⁻ | add dilute hydrochloric acid, then bubble any gas produced through limewater | fizzing; limewater goes cloudy (white precipitate) | CO₂; CaCO₃ (with limewater) |
| SO₄²⁻ | add dilute hydrochloric acid followed by barium chloride solution | white precipitate | BaSO₄ |
| Cl⁻ | add dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution | white precipitate | AgCl |
| Br⁻ | add dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution | cream precipitate | AgBr |
| I⁻ | add dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution | yellow precipitate | AgI |

Read the table by columns as well as by rows. The **test** column has a
pattern: the acid always comes first (bodyguard duty, removing interfering
ions), then the specific reagent names the ion. The **result** column has
two whites — carbonate (through limewater's CaCO₃) and chloride (AgCl) —
which is why the acid-then-reagent order is not optional: the carbonate's
white precipitate only forms with limewater *after* the acid has already
signalled it by fizzing. The **product** column is the ionic-equation
vocabulary: CO₂, CaCO₃, BaSO₄, AgCl, AgBr, AgI.

The full-anion discipline the table encodes: acid first, reagent second,
colour third, equation fourth. The same discipline reappears if the question
hands you an *unknown* and two or three test results at once — work row by
row, eliminate as you go, and name the compound only when every row agrees.

:::exam-hint
Table-reconstruction questions on 2.48 are free marks if the rows live in
your hand; interpretation questions are the real game. A typical setup gives
a table of results for an unknown compound — sodium hydroxide added (no
visible reaction), dilute hydrochloric acid (no reaction), hydrochloric acid
then barium chloride (no reaction), nitric acid then silver nitrate (white
precipitate) — and asks what it proves. Row by row: not NH₄⁺ (no ammonia), no
carbonate (no fizz), no sulfate (no white BaSO₄), chloride present (white
AgCl). The answer is a chloride whose cation is not ammonium — for example
sodium chloride. Practise that elimination reading until the table reads like
a sentence.
:::

:::misconception
"Two white precipitates means the tests are unreliable." The two whites belong
to different scripts: carbonate's white is calcium carbonate *in limewater*,
after fizzing with hydrochloric acid; chloride's white is silver chloride
*in silver nitrate*, after acidifying with nitric acid. Different acids,
different reagents, different confirmations. An unknown cannot fake its way
across both scripts at once — which is exactly why the exam table asks for
the reagent column as well as the result column.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.48 summary items. Rebuild all five rows from
memory (ion, test, result, product); explain why the acid always comes first;
and interpret this mini-set cold — no fizz with HCl, no precipitate with HCl
then BaCl₂, cream precipitate with HNO₃ then AgNO₃. Name the anion and the
reagent that proved it.
:::

sections.title: End of Unit 2
sections.markdown:
This section closes the chapter — and with it, Unit 2. Everything the chapter
taught now compresses into seven abilities, one per objective, and the unit's
question bank above (page anchor below the fold) is where each ability gets
its drills. The chapter's own questions do the same job at chapter scale: gas
identifications from single observations, full method descriptions for named
tests, and an unknown-compound interpretation that chains a precipitate
colour with an anion result — the exact shape the papers use.

:::summary
A [[chemical-test]] is one reagent, one observation, one conclusion. The five
gas tests: hydrogen — lighted splint, squeaky pop (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O); oxygen —
glowing splint, relights; carbon dioxide — limewater turns milky
(Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O, dissolving again to soluble calcium
hydrogencarbonate if bubbling continues); ammonia — damp red litmus turns
blue, the only alkaline gas; chlorine — damp blue litmus goes red then white
(acidic, then bleached). The [[flame-test]] cleans a platinum/nichrome wire
with concentrated hydrochloric acid, holds it in a non-luminous flame, and
reads five colours: Li⁺ red, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Cu²⁺
blue-green. Sodium hydroxide solution precipitates the metal hydroxides as coloured [[precipitate]]s —
Cu²⁺ blue, Fe²⁺ green (darkening to orange-brown on standing as air oxidises
it), Fe³⁺ orange-brown — and releases ammonia from ammonium salts
(NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O), confirmed on damp red litmus. The anion scripts:
carbonate — dilute hydrochloric acid fizzes, gas turns limewater milky
(CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O); sulfate — dilute hydrochloric acid then barium
chloride, white BaSO₄ (never sulfuric acid, nitric/barium nitrate as an
alternative pair); halides — acidify with nitric acid then silver nitrate,
AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow. Water: white anhydrous copper(II)
sulfate turns blue (presence); freezing at exactly 0 °C or boiling at exactly
100 °C proves purity — impure water freezes lower and boils higher.
:::

:::can-you
Keyed to the seven objectives, in order: give all five gas tests as
reagent-observation-conclusion scripts (2.44); describe the flame test method
in four moves with the cleaning rationale (2.45); reproduce the five-colour
table ion-to-colour and colour-to-ion (2.46); run all four sodium hydroxide
tests — three precipitate colours with ionic equations and the ammonium gas
test with its equation (2.47); execute all three anion scripts with their
acid-first rationales and the five-row summary table (2.48); state the
copper(II) sulfate water test and explain why it shows presence, not purity
(2.49); and give the physical purity test with both fixed points and both
drift directions (2.50).
:::

:::exam-hint
Every objective in this chapter is examined in both papers — no chemistry-only
content remains in Unit 2 after this chapter. The highest-yield revision
artefacts, in order: the cation summary table (four rows), the anion summary
table (five rows), and the five-colour flame table. The question types to
drill: single-observation gas identification; full method description with
state-symbol equations; and the multi-result unknown-compound interpretation,
where the marks go to row-by-row elimination. When describing any method,
number the steps — sequence marks are awarded in order and a scrambled
description strands them.
:::

:::misconception
"Each test is an isolated fact, so I revise them as twenty separate cards."
The tests interlock, and the interlocks are the exam questions. The ammonia
gas test *is* the confirmation step of the ammonium-ion test; the limewater
test *is* the confirmation step of the carbonate test; the acid-first habit
in the sulfate and halide scripts is one principle applied twice (destroy the
interfering anions before the specific reagent arrives); and the purity trap
binds the two water tests into one mark-scheme pair. Revise the tests as one
network with shared nodes and the unknown-compound questions become reading
comprehension instead of recall.
:::

:::cross-curricular
The chapter's opening idea — that routine analysis now belongs to machines —
describes real laboratories. Instrumental methods (flame photometry and its
descendants) do the flame test's job with detectors that read emission lines
the eye cannot separate, and they measure *how much* as well as *which*.
Yet the classical tests here remain the first line of field chemistry:
water-quality kits still carry the precipitation reagents, environmental
screening still begins with the colour of a precipitate, and the chlorine
bleach reaction you scripted is the same chemistry that makes chlorine the
workhorse of water treatment. Fast, cheap, interpretable by eye — the
twenty-first-century lab carries both toolkits and knows when each is the
right one.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.44–2.50 close-out items. Run the seven-ability
self-test in the can-you list above cold, in order, and flag any ability you
cannot state in one sentence — that flag is your revision list for this
chapter. The unit's question bank (page anchor above) supplies the drills for
each ability, and Unit 3 — energetics, rates and equilibrium, and the
organic chemistry that follows — opens with chemistry that leans on the
identification skills you just secured.
:::
